title: Ἀπόλλων ἐπὶ πύργου
about: Apollo carries out Zeus’ order: he lifts Sarpedon out of the missiles, bathes and anoints him, clothes him in deathless garments, and has Sleep and Death carry him to Lycia. Patroclus, who has not kept Achilles’ word, goes after the Trojans and Lycians, and the narrator says that the mind of Zeus is always stronger than that of men. Three times Patroclus goes up onto a corner of Troy’s wall, and three times Apollo thrusts him back; at the fourth rush the god warns him that Troy will not fall to him, and he gives way. Hector, unsure at the Scaean Gates whether to fight or to call the army behind the wall, is urged by Apollo, in the likeness of his uncle Asius, to drive at Patroclus. Patroclus leaps from his chariot and kills Hector’s charioteer Cebriones with a stone, taunts him as a diver, and the two heroes fight over the body, while the armies clash around them like winds in a forest.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἄρα πατρὸς ἀνηκούστησεν Ἀπόλλων.
βῆ δὲ κατ’ Ἰδαίων ὀρέων ἐς φύλοπιν αἰνήν,
αὐτίκα δ’ ἐκ βελέων Σαρπηδόνα δῖον ἀείρας
πολλὸν ἀπὸ πρὸ φέρων λοῦσεν ποταμοῖο ῥοῇσι
χρῖσέν τ’ ἀμβροσίῃ, περὶ δ’ ἄμβροτα εἵματα ἕσσε·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and not at all did Apollo fail to listen to his father.
And he went down from the Idaean mountains into the fearsome battle-din,
and at once, out of the missiles, heavenly Sarpedon having lifted,
far away bearing him, he bathed him in the streams of the river
and anointed him with ambrosia, and about him deathless garments put;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Apollo did not fail to listen to his father. He went down from the Idaean mountains into the fearsome din of battle, and at once lifted heavenly Sarpedon out of the missiles, carried him far away, bathed him in the streams of the river, anointed him with ambrosia, and put deathless garments about him;
sentences.n: Apollo carries out Zeus’ order of 16.667–670; lines 679–680 repeat 669–670 with aorists for the imperatives. The first line is the line of 15.236, where Apollo also obeys his father: ἀνηκούστησεν ‘did not fail to listen’ (ἀνηκουστέω) takes the genitive πατρός. βῆ is ‘went’ without the augment, and κατ’ Ἰδαίων ὀρέων is ‘down from the Idaean mountains’. ἀείρας is the aorist participle of ἀείρω ‘lift’. λοῦσεν ‘bathed’ and χρῖσεν ‘anointed’ are aorists, and περὶ … ἕσσε, with the preverb apart from its verb (tmesis), is ‘put about him’. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
πέμπε δέ μιν πομποῖσιν ἅμα κραιπνοῖσι φέρεσθαι,
ὕπνῳ καὶ θανάτῳ διδυμάοσιν, οἵ ῥά μιν ὦκα
κάτθεσαν ἐν Λυκίης εὐρείης πίονι δήμῳ.
sentences.l:
and sent him with escorts, rushing ones, to be borne,
with Sleep and Death, twins, who him quickly
set down in the rich land of wide Lycia.
sentences.i: and sent him to be carried with rushing escorts, with Sleep and Death, the twins, who quickly set him down in the rich land of wide Lycia.
sentences.n: The escorts Zeus named are sent. These lines are 16.671–673 word for word except the last verb: Zeus said θήσουσ’ ‘will set’, and here κάτθεσαν, the aorist of κατατίθημι with its preverb shortened, says they ‘set down’ (πέμπε is the imperfect ‘sent’, where at 671 it was an imperative). πομποῖσιν κραιπνοῖσι are ‘rushing escorts’, ὕπνῳ καὶ θανάτῳ διδυμάοσιν ‘Sleep and Death, twins’, and Λυκίης εὐρείης keeps its stock epithet ‘wide Lycia’.

sentences.t:
Πάτροκλος δ’ ἵπποισι καὶ Αὐτομέδοντι κελεύσας
Τρῶας καὶ Λυκίους μετεκίαθε, καὶ μέγ’ ἀάσθη
νήπιος·
sentences.i: But Patroclus gave his orders to the horses and to Automedon and went after the Trojans and the Lycians, and was struck with a great blindness of mind, foolish as he was;
sentences.n: The narrator turns from Sarpedon to Patroclus and passes judgement on him. κελεύσας, the aorist participle of κελεύω ‘order’, takes the dative ἵπποισι καὶ Αὐτομέδοντι; Automedon drives for Patroclus. μετεκίαθε is ‘went after’, from the rare μετακιαθέω. μέγ’ ἀάσθη, the aorist passive of ἀάω ‘blind the mind’, is the phrase used of Ajax at Odyssey 4.503, and νήπιος ‘foolish’ is the narrator’s comment, ‘foolish as he was’ in the free English. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
εἰ δὲ ἔπος Πηληϊάδαο φύλαξεν
ἦ τ’ ἂν ὑπέκφυγε κῆρα κακὴν μέλανος θανάτοιο.
sentences.l:
if he had kept the word of Peleus’-son,
truly he would have escaped the evil death-fate of black death.
sentences.i: If he had kept the word of the son of Peleus, he would surely have escaped the evil spirit of black death.
sentences.n: What would have saved him: Achilles’ order not to fight on toward Troy (16.87–96). εἰ δὲ … φύλαξεν is a past unreal condition, ‘if he had kept’, with the aorist φύλαξεν lacking its augment, and ἦ τ’ ἂν ὑπέκφυγε ‘surely he would have escaped’ is the result. ἔπος Πηληϊάδαο is ‘the word of Peleus’ son’, Πηληϊάδαο being the genitive of Πηληϊάδης. κῆρα κακὴν μέλανος θανάτοιο is ‘the evil death-fate of black death’: κήρ here is the spirit of death, not κῆρ ‘heart’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ αἰεί τε Διὸς κρείσσων νόος ἠέ περ ἀνδρῶν·
sentences.l: But always of Zeus stronger is the mind than that of men indeed;
sentences.i: But the mind of Zeus is always stronger than that of men;
sentences.n: A general truth, given as the cause of Patroclus’ ruin. αἰεί τε is ‘always’, the τε marking a general statement. Διὸς … νόος is ‘the mind of Zeus’, κρείσσων ‘stronger’ the comparative, and ἠέ περ ἀνδρῶν ‘than that of men indeed’, the noun νόος being understood with the genitive ἀνδρῶν.

sentences.t:
ὅς τε καὶ ἄλκιμον ἄνδρα φοβεῖ καὶ ἀφείλετο νίκην
ῥηϊδίως, ὅτε δ’ αὐτὸς ἐποτρύνῃσι μάχεσθαι·
sentences.l:
who both the valiant man puts to flight and takes away victory
easily, when he himself urges him on to fight;
sentences.i: who puts even the valiant man to flight and easily takes his victory away, when he himself urges him on to fight;
sentences.n: ὅς ‘who’ may refer to Zeus or to his mind, both masculine; the next line makes Zeus the doer, and the English reads ‘who’ as Zeus. φοβεῖ is ‘puts to flight’ (φοβέω, the causative of ‘fear’), and ἀφείλετο ‘takes away’ is an aorist used for a general truth, like the present beside it. ἄλκιμον ἄνδρα is ‘the valiant man’, ῥηϊδίως ‘easily’. ὅτε δ’ ἐποτρύνῃσι, with the subjunctive in -ῃσι and no ἄν, is a general ‘whenever … he urges’.

sentences.t: ὅς οἱ καὶ τότε θυμὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἀνῆκεν.
sentences.l: who for him also then the spirit in his chest urged on.
sentences.i: who also then urged on the spirit in his chest.
sentences.n: Zeus’ doing in Patroclus’ own case. ὅς is the same ‘who’, and οἱ ‘for him’ is Patroclus. ἀνῆκεν is the aorist of ἀνίημι ‘let go, send up’, which with θυμόν is ‘urged on’ the spirit; καὶ τότε ‘also then’ points back to the general rule just stated: what Zeus does to any man he did to Patroclus too, at that moment. ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν is ‘in the chest’, the plural στήθεσσι being the epic dative ending.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα τίνα πρῶτον τίνα δ’ ὕστατον ἐξενάριξας
Πατρόκλεις, ὅτε δή σε θεοὶ θάνατον δὲ κάλεσσαν;
sentences.l:
There whom first, whom last did you despoil,
Patroclus, when the gods called you to death?
sentences.i: Then whom did you first kill and strip of his armour, and whom last, Patroclus, when the gods called you to death?
sentences.n: The narrator speaks to Patroclus directly, as at 16.20, and asks which men he killed first and which last; the same question stands at 5.703 and 11.299. ἐξενάριξας is the aorist of ἐξεναρίζω ‘kill and strip’. Πατρόκλεις is the vocative, a shorter form than Πατρόκλεες (744, 754). θάνατον δέ is ‘to death’, with the suffix -δε of direction, and κάλεσσαν the aorist of καλέω ‘call’. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
Ἄδρηστον μὲν πρῶτα καὶ Αὐτόνοον καὶ Ἔχεκλον
καὶ Πέριμον Μεγάδην καὶ Ἐπίστορα καὶ Μελάνιππον,
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτ’ Ἔλασον καὶ Μούλιον ἠδὲ Πυλάρτην·
τοὺς ἕλεν·
sentences.i: Adrastus first, and Autonous and Echeclus, and Perimus, son of Megas, and Epistor and Melanippus, but then Elasus and Mulius and Pylartes: these he killed;
sentences.n: The answer is a list of nine victims, μέν answered by αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα (‘first … but then’); the verb waits until τοὺς ἕλεν ‘these he took’, ἕλεν being the aorist of αἱρέω, here ‘took’ in the sense of killed. Μεγάδην is a patronymic in form, ‘son of Megas’, set beside Πέριμον (the usual explanation). These lines say nothing more about any of the nine. The unit ends in the middle of the line.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ἄλλοι φύγαδε μνώοντο ἕκαστος.
sentences.l: and the others to flight were thinking, each one.
sentences.i: while each of the others thought of flight.
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ἄλλοι ‘and the others’ are those Patroclus did not kill; οἳ is the article used as a pronoun. φύγαδε is ‘to flight’, with the suffix -δε of direction, and μνώοντο is the imperfect of μνάομαι ‘think of’, uncontracted, here with φύγαδε ‘to flight’ (the thought turned toward flight); at 771 the same verb takes the genitive φόβοιο. ἕκαστος, ‘each one’, is singular after the plural verb.

sentences.t:
ἔνθά κεν ὑψίπυλον Τροίην ἕλον υἷες Ἀχαιῶν
Πατρόκλου ὑπὸ χερσί, περὶ πρὸ γὰρ ἔγχεϊ θῦεν,
εἰ μὴ Ἀπόλλων Φοῖβος ἐϋδμήτου ἐπὶ πύργου
ἔστη τῷ ὀλοὰ φρονέων, Τρώεσσι δ’ ἀρήγων.
sentences.l:
There would have taken high-gated Troy the sons of the Achaeans
under the hands of Patroclus, for far ahead with the spear he raged,
if not Apollo Phoebus, upon the well-built tower
had stood against him, baneful things thinking, and the Trojans helping.
sentences.i: Then the sons of the Achaeans would have taken high-gated Troy at the hands of Patroclus, for he raged with his spear far in front, if Phoebus Apollo had not taken his stand against him on the well-built tower, with baneful thoughts, and helping the Trojans.
sentences.n: Without the god, Troy would have fallen to Patroclus. ἔνθά κεν … ἕλον is a past unreal, ‘would have taken’, with ὑψίπυλον Τροίην ‘high-gated Troy’ as object and υἷες Ἀχαιῶν as subject. περὶ πρὸ γὰρ ἔγχεϊ θῦεν is the line of 11.180 with a new subject: the pair περὶ πρό is not understood, and ‘far in front’ is a guess. εἰ μὴ … ἔστη completes the condition; ὀλοά is the neuter plural ‘baneful things’ with φρονέων ‘thinking’, and τῷ is ‘against him’. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
τρὶς μὲν ἐπ’ ἀγκῶνος βῆ τείχεος ὑψηλοῖο
Πάτροκλος, τρὶς δ’ αὐτὸν ἀπεστυφέλιξεν Ἀπόλλων
χείρεσσ’ ἀθανάτῃσι φαεινὴν ἀσπίδα νύσσων.
sentences.l:
Three times indeed upon the elbow of the high wall went up
Patroclus, and three times him thrust back Apollo,
with immortal hands striking the shining shield.
sentences.i: Three times Patroclus went up onto a jutting corner of the high wall, and three times Apollo drove him back, striking his shining shield with his immortal hands.
sentences.n: Three attempts and a god who stops each of them: the pattern, and the fourth rush of the next line, are those of 5.436–438, where Apollo turns Diomedes back. ἀγκών is ‘elbow’, here a jutting corner or angle of the wall (the usual explanation; the exact structure is not known). ἀπεστυφέλιξεν is ‘thrust back’, and νύσσων, ‘striking’, is the participle of νύσσω ‘prick, stab’, used here of a blow with the hands. χείρεσσ’ ἀθανάτῃσι is ‘with immortal hands’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ τὸ τέταρτον ἐπέσσυτο δαίμονι ἶσος,
δεινὰ δ’ ὁμοκλήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
But when for the fourth time he rushed on, equal to a divinity,
and dreadfully having shouted at him, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: But when he rushed on for the fourth time, like a divinity, Apollo shouted dreadfully at him and spoke winged words:
sentences.n: Apollo is not named in these lines: he is the subject of προσηύδα (last named at 703), and the free English names him. Patroclus is the subject of ἐπέσσυτο ‘rushed on’, δαίμονι ἶσος ‘like a divinity’ being said of him. The first line is the line of 5.438, and δεινὰ δ’ ὁμοκλήσας is the half-line of 5.439, where Diomedes is turned back; δεινά is the neuter plural as an adverb, ‘dreadfully’. ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the stock ‘spoke winged words’.

sentences.t:
χάζεο διογενὲς Πατρόκλεες· οὔ νύ τοι αἶσα
σῷ ὑπὸ δουρὶ πόλιν πέρθαι Τρώων ἀγερώχων,
οὐδ’ ὑπ’ Ἀχιλλῆος, ὅς περ σέο πολλὸν ἀμείνων.
sentences.l:
“Give ground, Zeus-sprung Patroclus; not now for you is it the portion
under your spear the city to sack of the lofty Trojans,
nor under Achilles, who indeed is much better than you.”
sentences.i: “Give ground, Zeus-born Patroclus: it is not your lot to sack the city of the lofty Trojans under your spear, nor under Achilles, though he is far better than you.”
sentences.n: Apollo warns Patroclus: Troy will not fall to him, nor even to Achilles. χάζεο is the imperative of χάζομαι ‘give ground’, with the uncontracted ending -εο, and διογενές is the stock address ‘Zeus-sprung’. οὔ νύ τοι αἶσα has no verb: ‘it is not your portion’, τοι standing for σοι, with the infinitive πέρθαι ‘to sack’. ἀγερώχων, ‘lofty’, is a word whose meaning is not known. ὅς περ σέο … ἀμείνων is ‘who indeed is better than you’, σέο being the genitive of comparison.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, Πάτροκλος δ’ ἀνεχάζετο πολλὸν ὀπίσσω
μῆνιν ἀλευάμενος ἑκατηβόλου Ἀπόλλωνος.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and Patroclus drew back far, backward,
avoiding the wrath of far-shooting Apollo.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Patroclus drew back a long way, avoiding the wrath of Apollo, who shoots from afar.
sentences.n: Patroclus yields to the god, though he had not kept Achilles’ word (686–687). These are the lines of 5.443–444, where Diomedes yields, with Πάτροκλος for Τυδεΐδης and πολλόν ‘a long way’ for τυτθόν ‘a little’. ἀνεχάζετο is the imperfect of ἀναχάζομαι ‘draw back’, and ἀλευάμενος the aorist participle of ἀλέομαι ‘avoid’. μῆνιν is the ‘wrath’ of the first word of the poem, here a god’s, and ἑκατηβόλου is ‘far-shooting’. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ δ’ ἐν Σκαιῇσι πύλῃς ἔχε μώνυχας ἵππους·
δίζε γὰρ ἠὲ μάχοιτο κατὰ κλόνον αὖτις ἐλάσσας,
ἦ λαοὺς ἐς τεῖχος ὁμοκλήσειεν ἀλῆναι.
sentences.i: Hector was holding his solid-hoofed horses at the Scaean Gates, for he was in two minds whether to drive back into the turmoil and fight again, or to call the people with a shout to crowd into the wall.
sentences.n: Hector waits at the Scaean Gates, unsure whether to go back into the fighting or call the army behind the wall. Σκαιαί … πύλαι, the Scaean Gates, is a name kept as a name; its meaning is a guess. ἔχε is ‘held’, and μώνυχας ‘solid-hoofed’ is the stock epithet of horses. δίζε is the imperfect of δίζω ‘be in two minds’ (formed on δίς ‘twice’), followed by the optatives μάχοιτο and ὁμοκλήσειεν, ‘whether he should fight … or call’. ἐλάσσας is the aorist participle of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’. ἀλῆναι is the aorist passive infinitive of εἰλέω ‘crowd together’. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
ταῦτ’ ἄρα οἱ φρονέοντι παρίστατο Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων
ἀνέρι εἰσάμενος αἰζηῷ τε κρατερῷ τε
Ἀσίῳ, ὃς μήτρως ἦν Ἕκτορος ἱπποδάμοιο
αὐτοκασίγνητος Ἑκάβης, υἱὸς δὲ Δύμαντος,
ὃς Φρυγίῃ ναίεσκε ῥοῇς ἔπι Σαγγαρίοιο·
sentences.l:
These things, as he was thinking them, stood beside him Phoebus Apollo,
making himself like a man, vigorous and strong,
Asius, who was mother’s-brother of Hector, horse-taming,
own brother of Hecuba, and son of Dymas,
who in Phrygia lived by the streams of the Sangarius;
sentences.i: While he was thinking this over, Phoebus Apollo stood beside him, taking the likeness of a vigorous, strong man, Asius, the mother’s brother of Hector, tamer of horses, own brother of Hecuba and son of Dymas, who used to live in Phrygia by the streams of the Sangarius;
sentences.n: Apollo appears to Hector in the likeness of his uncle Asius, Hecuba’s brother; μήτρως is the mother’s brother. παρίστατο is ‘stood beside’, with οἱ φρονέοντι ‘to him as he thought’. εἰσάμενος, ‘making himself like’, is the aorist participle of εἴδομαι, with the dative ἀνέρι … Ἀσίῳ. αἰζηῷ is taken as the adjective ‘vigorous’ rather than ‘vigorous young man’, since Asius is Hecuba’s brother. ναίεσκε is an imperfect with the suffix -εσκε, ‘used to live’.

sentences.t: τῷ μιν ἐεισάμενος προσέφη Διὸς υἱὸς Ἀπόλλων·
sentences.l: Having made himself like to that man, addressed him Zeus’ son Apollo:
sentences.i: Making himself like that man, Apollo, the son of Zeus, said to him:
sentences.n: Apollo speaks to Hector in Asius’ likeness. τῷ ‘to him’ is Asius, whom the god imitates, and μιν ‘him’ is Hector, who is addressed: the two are different people, and the free English reads τῷ as ‘that man’. ἐεισάμενος is ‘making himself like’, and προσέφη the aorist of πρόσφημι ‘spoke to’. Διὸς υἱός is ‘son of Zeus’.

sentences.t: Ἕκτορ τίπτε μάχης ἀποπαύεαι; οὐδέ τί σε χρή.
sentences.l: “Hector, why from battle do you cease? Not at all is it needful for you.
sentences.i: “Hector, why are you leaving off from the battle? There is no need at all for you.
sentences.n: Apollo asks Hector why he is holding back, and says he need not. τίπτε is τί ποτε ‘why ever’. ἀποπαύεαι is the present middle of ἀποπαύω, ‘cease from’ (with the genitive μάχης ‘from battle’), with the uncontracted ending -εαι. οὐδέ τί σε χρή is ‘it is not at all needful for you’, the infinitive being understood from the question.

sentences.t:
αἴθ’ ὅσον ἥσσων εἰμί, τόσον σέο φέρτερος εἴην·
τώ κε τάχα στυγερῶς πολέμου ἀπερωήσειας.
sentences.l:
If only as much as I am weaker, so much than you stronger I were;
then soon hatefully from war you would draw back.
sentences.i: If only I were as much stronger than you as I am weaker; then you would soon draw back from war, hatefully.
sentences.n: A wish: if the speaker were as much stronger than Hector as he is weaker, Hector would be forced from the war. αἴθε is ‘if only’, and ὅσον … τόσον ‘as much as … so much’ pairs ἥσσων ‘weaker’ with φέρτερος ‘stronger’, σέο being the genitive of comparison and εἴην a wishing optative. τώ is τῷ ‘in that case’, and κε … ἀπερωήσειας ‘you would draw back’ (ἀπερωέω, with the genitive πολέμου). στυγερῶς is ‘hatefully’; its force here is not certain.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε Πατρόκλῳ ἔφεπε κρατερώνυχας ἵππους,
αἴ κέν πώς μιν ἕλῃς, δώῃ δέ τοι εὖχος Ἀπόλλων.
sentences.l:
But come, at Patroclus drive the strong-hoofed horses,
if in some way him you may take, and may give you a boast Apollo.”
sentences.i: But come, drive your strong-hoofed horses at Patroclus, in case you can somehow take him, and Apollo may give you the triumph.”
sentences.n: The advice itself: drive at Patroclus. ἄγε is ‘come’, ἔφεπε the imperative of ἐφέπω ‘drive at’ with the dative Πατρόκλῳ, and κρατερώνυχας ‘strong-hoofed’ the epithet of horses. αἴ κέν … ἕλῃς, with the aorist subjunctive of αἱρέω, is ‘in case you can take him’, δώῃ ‘may give’ is the subjunctive of δίδωμι, and εὖχος is ‘a boast’ in the literal English, ‘the triumph’ in the free English. The god who speaks is the one who will help Hector win it.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν ὃ μὲν αὖτις ἔβη θεὸς ἂμ πόνον ἀνδρῶν,
Κεβριόνῃ δ’ ἐκέλευσε δαΐφρονι φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ
ἵππους ἐς πόλεμον πεπληγέμεν.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the god went back again into the toil of men; and glorious Hector ordered wise-hearted Cebriones to lash the horses into the war.
sentences.n: Apollo leaves, and Hector orders his charioteer forward. The first line is the line of 13.239, which closes a god’s disguised speech there. Κεβριόνῃ δαΐφρονι is the dative after ἐκέλευσε ‘ordered’; Cebriones is Hector’s charioteer and a son of Priam (737–738), and δαΐφρων is ‘wise-minded’ or ‘fierce’, the sense being disputed. πεπληγέμεν is the infinitive of the reduplicated aorist of πλήσσω ‘strike’, here with a whip. A new paragraph begins here. The unit ends in the middle of line 728.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀπόλλων
δύσεθ’ ὅμιλον ἰών, ἐν δὲ κλόνον Ἀργείοισιν
ἧκε κακόν, Τρωσὶν δὲ καὶ Ἕκτορι κῦδος ὄπαζεν.
sentences.l:
But Apollo
entered the throng, going, and among the Argives a turmoil
sent, an evil one, and to the Trojans and to Hector glory he was granting.
sentences.i: But Apollo went into the throng and sent an evil turmoil among the Argives, and granted glory to the Trojans and to Hector.
sentences.n: Apollo now works for the Trojans. δύσεθ’ is the aorist middle of δύω ‘go into’, unaugmented, and ἐν … ἧκε, with the preverb apart from its verb (tmesis), is ‘sent among’: κλόνον κακόν is ‘an evil turmoil’ and Ἀργείοισιν ‘the Argives’. κῦδος ὄπαζεν is ‘was granting glory’, the imperfect of ὀπάζω, with the datives Τρωσὶν … καὶ Ἕκτορι. The unit begins in the middle of line 728.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ δ’ ἄλλους μὲν Δαναοὺς ἔα οὐδ’ ἐνάριζεν·
αὐτὰρ ὃ Πατρόκλῳ ἔφεπε κρατερώνυχας ἵππους.
sentences.l:
And Hector the other Danaans indeed let be, and was not despoiling them;
but he at Patroclus drove the strong-hoofed horses.
sentences.i: Hector let the other Danaans be and did not strip them of their armour, but drove his strong-hoofed horses at Patroclus.
sentences.n: Hector does as Apollo advised. ἔα is the imperfect of ἐάω ‘let be’, and ἐνάριζεν the imperfect of ἐναρίζω ‘strip a slain man’; since stripping follows killing, ‘he was not despoiling them’ means he made no kills among them. The second line repeats 724 after its first two words (ἀλλ’ ἄγε there, αὐτὰρ ὃ here), with ἔφεπε now an indicative, the imperfect: Πατρόκλῳ ἔφεπε κρατερώνυχας ἵππους.

sentences.t:
Πάτροκλος δ’ ἑτέρωθεν ἀφ’ ἵππων ἆλτο χαμᾶζε
σκαιῇ ἔγχος ἔχων· ἑτέρηφι δὲ λάζετο πέτρον
μάρμαρον ὀκριόεντα τόν οἱ περὶ χεὶρ ἐκάλυψεν,
sentences.l:
And Patroclus, on the other side, from the horses leapt to the ground,
in his left the spear holding; and in the other he took a stone,
a rock, jagged, which his hand around covered,
sentences.i: On the other side Patroclus leapt from his chariot to the ground, holding his spear in his left hand; with the other he took up a stone, a jagged rock, which his hand covered all round,
sentences.n: Patroclus meets the chariot on foot. ἑτέρωθεν is ‘on the other side’, and ἀφ’ ἵππων ἆλτο χαμᾶζε is ‘leapt from the horses (the chariot) to the ground’, ἆλτο being the aorist of ἅλλομαι. σκαιῇ is ‘in the left’ (hand), ἑτέρηφι ‘in the other’ with the ending -φι, and λάζετο ‘took’. πέτρον … μάρμαρον ὀκριόεντα is ‘a stone, a rock, jagged’; μάρμαρος is any hard rock, not yet ‘marble’. τόν οἱ περὶ χεὶρ ἐκάλυψεν says the stone just filled his hand. The unit ends at a comma, since the sentence runs on for four more lines.

sentences.t:
ἧκε δ’ ἐρεισάμενος, οὐδὲ δὴν χάζετο φωτός,
οὐδ’ ἁλίωσε βέλος, βάλε δ’ Ἕκτορος ἡνιοχῆα
Κεβριόνην νόθον υἱὸν ἀγακλῆος Πριάμοιο
ἵππων ἡνί’ ἔχοντα μετώπιον ὀξέϊ λᾶϊ.
sentences.l:
and sent it, bracing himself, and not for long did he give ground from the man,
nor did he make the missile vain, but struck Hector’s charioteer
Cebriones, a bastard son of renowned Priam,
the reins of the horses holding, on the forehead with a sharp stone.
sentences.i: and sent it, bracing himself, and did not give ground before the man for long, nor did the missile fail: he struck Hector’s charioteer Cebriones, an illegitimate son of renowned Priam, who was holding the reins of the horses, on the forehead with the sharp stone.
sentences.n: The throw lands on the charioteer. ἧκε is ‘sent’ (the stone), ἐρεισάμενος ‘bracing himself’, and οὐδὲ δὴν χάζετο φωτός ‘and not for long did he give ground from the man’; the Greek does not say whether the man is Hector or his charioteer. οὐδ’ ἁλίωσε βέλος is ‘nor did he make the missile vain’, βέλος here being the thrown stone. νόθον υἱὸν is ‘an illegitimate son’, ἀγακλῆος ‘renowned’ (epic -ῆος for -έους), ἡνιοχῆα ‘charioteer’, and ὀξέϊ λᾶϊ ‘with a sharp stone’, λᾶϊ being the dative of λᾶας.

sentences.t:
ἀμφοτέρας δ’ ὀφρῦς σύνελεν λίθος, οὐδέ οἱ ἔσχεν
ὀστέον, ὀφθαλμοὶ δὲ χαμαὶ πέσον ἐν κονίῃσιν
αὐτοῦ πρόσθε ποδῶν·
sentences.i: The stone crushed both his brows together and the bone did not hold, and his eyes fell to the ground in the dust, right there before his feet;
sentences.n: The blow is told without softening. σύνελεν is the aorist of συναιρέω ‘crush together’, and ἔσχεν, ‘held’, has ὀστέον ‘bone’ as its subject, the sense being that the bone did not hold out. πέσον is the aorist of πίπτω without the augment; χαμαί is ‘to the ground’ and ἐν κονίῃσιν ‘in the dust’, with the plural -ῃσιν. αὐτοῦ is ‘right there’, and πρόσθε ποδῶν ‘before his feet’.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ ἀρνευτῆρι ἐοικὼς
κάππεσ’ ἀπ’ εὐεργέος δίφρου, λίπε δ’ ὀστέα θυμός.
sentences.l:
and he, like a diver,
fell down from the well-made chariot, and left his bones the spirit.
sentences.i: and he, like a diver, fell from the well-made chariot, and his spirit left his bones.
sentences.n: Cebriones falls ‘like a diver’, the image Patroclus picks up in his taunt. These are the words of 12.385–386, with ‘chariot’ for ‘high tower’. ἀρνευτῆρι ἐοικώς is ‘like a diver’, and κάππεσ’ is κατέπεσε, ‘fell down’, with the preverb shortened to match the next consonant. εὐεργέος δίφρου is ‘well-made chariot’, and λίπε δ’ ὀστέα θυμός, in the order of the Greek ‘left his bones the spirit’, is ‘his spirit left his bones’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἐπικερτομέων προσέφης Πατρόκλεες ἱππεῦ·
sentences.l: Him, taunting, you addressed, Patroclus the horseman:
sentences.i: Taunting him, you said to him, Patroclus the horseman:
sentences.n: Patroclus’ speech is introduced, the narrator again speaking to him as at 16.20. ἐπικερτομέων is the participle of ἐπικερτομέω ‘taunt’, and προσέφης is the second-person aorist ‘you addressed’, where the formula usually has a third person. Πατρόκλεες ἱππεῦ is ‘Patroclus the horseman’.

sentences.t: ὢ πόποι ἦ μάλ’ ἐλαφρὸς ἀνήρ, ὡς ῥεῖα κυβιστᾷ.
sentences.l: “Ah! truly very light is the man, how easily he tumbles!
sentences.i: “Ah, truly, what a light man he is, and how easily he tumbles!
sentences.n: The taunt plays on ‘diver’: Cebriones has dived from his chariot. ὢ πόποι is ‘Ah’, ἦ μάλ’ ‘truly very’, and ἐλαφρός is ‘light’, here ‘nimble’. κυβιστᾷ is the present of κυβιστάω ‘tumble head over heels’, a word also used of diving; ῥεῖα is ‘easily’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δή που καὶ πόντῳ ἐν ἰχθυόεντι γένοιτο,
πολλοὺς ἂν κορέσειεν ἀνὴρ ὅδε τήθεα διφῶν
νηὸς ἀποθρῴσκων, εἰ καὶ δυσπέμφελος εἴη,
ὡς νῦν ἐν πεδίῳ ἐξ ἵππων ῥεῖα κυβιστᾷ.
sentences.l:
If indeed somewhere on the fish-teeming sea he were,
many this man would satisfy, oysters searching for,
leaping from a ship, even if rough it were,
as now on the plain from the horses easily he tumbles.
sentences.i: If he were somewhere on the fish-teeming sea, this man would feed many, searching for oysters as he leaps from a ship, even if the sea were rough, just as now on the plain he so easily tumbles from his chariot.
sentences.n: The mockery goes on: on the sea this man would feed many by diving. εἰ … γένοιτο … ἂν κορέσειεν is a less vivid condition, ‘if he were … he would feed’, with κορέσειεν ‘satisfy’ and πολλούς ‘many’. τήθεα is taken as ‘oysters’, and διφῶν ‘searching for’ and ἀποθρῴσκων ‘leaping from’ are present participles. ἰχθυόεντι ‘fish-teeming’ is the sea’s stock epithet, and δυσπέμφελος is ‘rough’ of the sea.

sentences.t: ἦ ῥα καὶ ἐν Τρώεσσι κυβιστητῆρες ἔασιν.
sentences.l: Truly then, among the Trojans too there are tumblers.”
sentences.i: Truly, there are tumblers among the Trojans, too.”
sentences.n: The taunt ends. ἦ ῥα here is ‘truly, then’, not the ἦ ῥα καί of the narrative formula ‘so he said, and’; καί means ‘too’ with ἐν Τρώεσσι ‘among the Trojans’. κυβιστητῆρες ‘tumblers’ is built on κυβιστάω, and ἔασιν is the epic form of εἰσίν.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν ἐπὶ Κεβριόνῃ ἥρωϊ βεβήκει
οἶμα λέοντος ἔχων, ὅς τε σταθμοὺς κεραΐζων
ἔβλητο πρὸς στῆθος, ἑή τέ μιν ὤλεσεν ἀλκή·
ὣς ἐπὶ Κεβριόνῃ Πατρόκλεες ἆλσο μεμαώς.
sentences.l:
So having spoken, upon Cebriones the hero he had come,
the rush of a lion having, who, the steadings ravaging,
was struck in the chest, and his own might destroyed him;
so upon Cebriones, Patroclus, you leapt, eager.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and advanced on the hero Cebriones with the rush of a lion, who, ravaging the steadings, was struck in the chest, and his own might destroyed him; so, Patroclus, you leapt upon Cebriones, eager.
sentences.n: Patroclus goes for the body, like a lion. βεβήκει is the pluperfect of βαίνω, ‘had gone, advanced’. οἶμα λέοντος is ‘the rush of a lion’ (οἶμα is rare; ‘rush’ is the usual explanation). ὅς τε σταθμοὺς κεραΐζων is ‘who, ravaging the steadings’, and the aorists in the simile, ἔβλητο and ὤλεσεν, tell what happens to such a lion; ἑή is the possessive ‘his own’, ἀλκή ‘might’. The narrator again speaks to Patroclus: ἆλσο is the aorist of ἅλλομαι, μεμαώς ‘eager’. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t: Ἕκτωρ δ’ αὖθ’ ἑτέρωθεν ἀφ’ ἵππων ἆλτο χαμᾶζε.
sentences.l: And Hector in turn, on the other side, from the horses leapt to the ground.
sentences.i: And Hector in turn leapt from his chariot to the ground on the other side.
sentences.n: Hector too dismounts, so that the two face each other on foot over the body. The line matches 733 with Hector for Patroclus and αὖθ’ added: αὖθ’ is αὖτε ‘in turn’, ἑτέρωθεν ‘on the other side’, and ἀφ’ ἵππων ἆλτο χαμᾶζε ‘leapt from the horses to the ground’.

sentences.t:
τὼ περὶ Κεβριόναο λέονθ’ ὣς δηρινθήτην,
ὥ τ’ ὄρεος κορυφῇσι περὶ κταμένης ἐλάφοιο
ἄμφω πεινάοντε μέγα φρονέοντε μάχεσθον·
sentences.i: The two contended over Cebriones like two lions that fight on the peaks of a mountain over a slain deer, both hungry, both full of proud thoughts;
sentences.n: A lion simile for Patroclus and Hector, and the Greek keeps the dual throughout: τὼ ‘the two’, λέονθ’ ‘two lions’, δηρινθήτην ‘they two contended’ (the aorist passive of δηριάομαι), ὥ τ’ ‘who two’, πεινάοντε, φρονέοντε and μάχεσθον. κορυφῇσι is ‘on the peaks’, κταμένης ἐλάφοιο ‘a slain deer’ (κταμένης, aorist participle of κτείνω), and μέγα φρονέοντε ‘with great thoughts’, i.e. proud ones. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: Κεβριόναο can be fitted to the verse only by counting its short syllable -να- long, in the third foot, and the fifth foot is a spondee (δηρινθήτην).

sentences.t:
ὣς περὶ Κεβριόναο δύω μήστωρες ἀϋτῆς
Πάτροκλός τε Μενοιτιάδης καὶ φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ
ἵεντ’ ἀλλήλων ταμέειν χρόα νηλέϊ χαλκῷ.
sentences.l:
So around Cebriones two counsellors of the battle-cry,
Patroclus, Menoetius’-son, and glorious Hector,
were eager of one another to cut the skin with pitiless bronze.
sentences.i: So over Cebriones the two masters of the battle-cry, Patroclus, son of Menoetius, and glorious Hector, were eager to cut one another’s skin with pitiless bronze.
sentences.n: The simile is applied to the two men. μήστωρες ἀϋτῆς, literally ‘counsellors of the battle-cry’, names fighters who are masters of the war-shout. Μενοιτιάδης is the patronymic ‘Menoetius’-son’. ἵεντ’ is ἵεντο ‘were eager’, plural after the two named subjects, with ἀλλήλων ‘of one another’. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: Κεβριόναο can be fitted to the verse only by counting its short syllable -να- long, in the third foot. The last line is the line of 13.501, said there of Aeneas and Idomeneus.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ μὲν κεφαλῆφιν ἐπεὶ λάβεν οὐχὶ μεθίει·
Πάτροκλος δ’ ἑτέρωθεν ἔχεν ποδός·
sentences.l:
Hector, indeed, when by the head he took hold, did not let go;
and Patroclus on the other side held him by the foot;
sentences.i: Hector, once he had taken hold of the head, did not let go, and Patroclus on the other side held on to the foot;
sentences.n: Each has hold of the body, Hector by the head and Patroclus by the foot; the dead man is not named in these lines. κεφαλῆφιν is ‘by the head’, with the ending -φι, and ποδός ‘by the foot’ is a genitive. ἐπεὶ λάβεν is ‘when he had taken’, and οὐχὶ μεθίει ‘did not let go’ is the imperfect of μεθίημι. ἔχεν is ‘held’, without the augment.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ δὴ ἄλλοι
Τρῶες καὶ Δαναοὶ σύναγον κρατερὴν ὑσμίνην.
sentences.l:
and the others then
Trojans and Danaans brought together strong battle.
sentences.i: and the others, Trojans and Danaans, joined in strong battle.
sentences.n: While the two hold the body, the armies fight round them. οἳ δὲ δὴ ἄλλοι ‘and the others then’ is the rest of the armies, named in apposition: Τρῶες καὶ Δαναοί. σύναγον is the imperfect of συνάγω ‘bring together’, without the augment. The second line is the line of 14.448.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ Εὖρός τε Νότος τ’ ἐριδαίνετον ἀλλήλοιιν
οὔρεος ἐν βήσσῃς βαθέην πελεμιζέμεν ὕλην
φηγόν τε μελίην τε τανύφλοιόν τε κράνειαν,
αἵ τε πρὸς ἀλλήλας ἔβαλον τανυήκεας ὄζους
ἠχῇ θεσπεσίῃ, πάταγος δέ τε ἀγνυμενάων,
sentences.l:
And as the East Wind and the South Wind quarrel with one another
in the glens of a mountain to shake the deep forest,
oak and ash and long-barked cornel,
which against one another cast their long-pointed boughs
with a wondrous din, and there is a crashing of them breaking,
sentences.i: And as the East Wind and the South Wind quarrel with one another in the glens of a mountain, to shake the deep forest, oak and ash and long-barked cornel, which cast their long-pointed boughs against one another with a wondrous din, and there is a crashing of them as they break,
sentences.n: A storm simile for the battle round the body; it runs on into the next unit (ὣς …, ‘so …’), and this unit ends at a comma because the sentence is long. ἐριδαίνετον and ἀλλήλοιιν are duals, ‘the two quarrel’ and ‘with one another’, and βήσσῃς is a dative plural in -ῃς, ‘in the glens’. φηγόν is an oak, not a beech, μελίην an ash, τανύφλοιον ‘long-barked’ and κράνειαν a cornel; the tree names are the usual identifications. τανυήκεας is ‘long-pointed’ (τανυ- ‘long’ with a second element usually taken as ἀκή ‘point’; not certain, and the Odyssey’s swords with the same adjective are ‘long-edged’), and ἀγνυμενάων ‘of them breaking’.

sentences.t:
ὣς Τρῶες καὶ Ἀχαιοὶ ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισι θορόντες
δῄουν, οὐδ’ ἕτεροι μνώοντ’ ὀλοοῖο φόβοιο.
sentences.l:
so Trojans and Achaeans, upon one another having leapt,
cut down, and neither side thought of baneful flight.
sentences.i: so Trojans and Achaeans leapt upon one another and cut each other down, and neither side gave a thought to baneful flight.
sentences.n: The simile is applied: the armies batter one another like the trees. Τρῶες καὶ Ἀχαιοί is the poet’s variation on ‘Trojans and Danaans’ of 764, the same army under another name. θορόντες is the aorist participle of θρῴσκω ‘leap’, and δῄουν the imperfect of δηϊόω ‘cut down’, without the augment. οὐδ’ ἕτεροι, ‘nor the others’, is ‘neither side’, and μνώοντ’ … ὀλοοῖο φόβοιο ‘thought of baneful flight’ uses the verb of 697, where it is said of the men Patroclus did not kill. The lines are those of 11.70–71.

sentences.t:
πολλὰ δὲ Κεβριόνην ἀμφ’ ὀξέα δοῦρα πεπήγει
ἰοί τε πτερόεντες ἀπὸ νευρῆφι θορόντες,
πολλὰ δὲ χερμάδια μεγάλ’ ἀσπίδας ἐστυφέλιξαν
μαρναμένων ἀμφ’ αὐτόν·
sentences.l:
And many sharp spears around Cebriones were fixed,
and winged arrows, from the bowstring having leapt,
and many rocks, great ones, thrust roughly the shields
of men fighting around him;
sentences.i: Many sharp spears were fixed around Cebriones, and winged arrows that had leapt from the bowstring, and many great rocks battered the shields of the men fighting around him;
sentences.n: What flies around the body. πεπήγει is the pluperfect of πήγνυμι ‘fix’, singular with the neuter plural δοῦρα, as Greek allows, and the arrows ἰοί … θορόντες ‘leaping’ share it. ἀπὸ νευρῆφι has the ending -φι, ‘from the bowstring’. ἐστυφέλιξαν is the aorist of στυφελίζω ‘thrust roughly’, said here of rocks striking shields and given as ‘battered’ in the free English; μαρναμένων ἀμφ’ αὐτόν ‘of those fighting around him’ depends on ἀσπίδας. The unit ends in the middle of line 775.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἐν στροφάλιγγι κονίης
κεῖτο μέγας μεγαλωστί, λελασμένος ἱπποσυνάων.
sentences.l:
and he in the whirl of dust
lay, great in his greatness, forgetful of his horsemanship.
sentences.i: and he lay in the whirl of dust, stretched out at full length, forgetful of his horsemanship.
sentences.n: The part closes on the fallen charioteer. The two lines are Odyssey 24.39–40, said there of Achilles’ body, with ὃ δ’ for σὺ δ’ and κεῖτο for κεῖσο. στροφάλιγγι is the dative of a noun with stem στροφαλιγγ- ‘whirl’, κονίης the Ionic genitive of κονία ‘dust’, and κεῖτο the imperfect of κεῖμαι ‘lay’. μέγας μεγαλωστί puts an adjective beside an adverb of the same root, ‘great in his greatness’, a body stretched out at length. λελασμένος is the perfect participle of λανθάνομαι ‘forget’, with the genitive ἱπποσυνάων, a charioteer’s skills.
